1263824,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.1.4.2,1942-04-22,396d7d47-d79c-4aea-bf33-18c3e7b199e3,ca.m.9501,Mr. ILSLEY:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,QUESTIONS,BANK OF CANADA-SHORT TERM SECURITIES,,The information asked for

in regard to Bank of Canada's holdings of specific securities is not of government record. The Bank of Canada Act sets forth the classes of securities which the bank may acquire and places limits on holdings of securities having a term longer than two years. Certain safeguards have therefore been prescribed by
Questions

parliament, but no statutory provision exists for the publication of a detailed list of securities held. It is not considered that the dissemination of such information would serve any public interest. It might, in fact, work against the public interest by disclosing information which might benefit a limited number of persons operating in the security markets. The latest weekly statement of the Bank of Canada (April 15, 1942) shows the following holdings of dominion and provincial securities, classified as to whether they mature within two years or after two years, as required by the Bank of Canada Act: dominion and provincial government short term securities, $382,172,082.77; other dominion and provincial government securities, $214,869.680.81; total, $597,041,763.58.

See sessional paper No. 177 for details of dominion of Canada bond issues sold since September 1, 1939, in the first instance to the Bank of Canada. (This does not, of course, mean that all such securities are now held by the Bank of Canada.)

RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):,Minister of National Defence,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,"Two or three questions were asked me the last day that matters connected with

the army were brought up. One was by the hon. member for Weyburn, with regard to a lease from the International Harvester Company of a building, in Weyburn I think it was. The hon. member had the idea, and so expressed it, that a building which had been leased by the department had been given up by the department and that when the manager of the company offered to allow the building to remain idle, so that it might be used again by the department, this offer was refused and the department insisted on carrying out the terms of the lease, which were that the department should put it in the same shape as it was prior to the leasing. He intimated that an expenditure of something like $2,000 had been made, and he said-I am reading from what he stated in the committee-at page 1665 of Hansard:

It seems to me that this was a case of red tape actually interfering in what would have been an ordinary, common sense business transaction of accepting the offer of the International Harvester Company to let the building stand idle, to waive the rent and storage charges, so that in the event of the building being required the arrangement could have been picked up again right where it was dropped.

I had inquiries made about it, and my hon. friend is to some extent correct, in his suggestion that the local manager of the company indicated that he thought possibly it could be arranged that t'he building might stand idle and the department would not necessarily have to carry out its obligation to put it back in the same shape as it was before; that, perhaps, was the substance of the conversation between the representative of the department and the local manager. The local manager, however, said that he would refer the matter to the headquarters of the company at Chicago, and later he wrote this letter, from which I will read, dated October 20, 194)1, addressed to Captain Evans, Department of National Defence, Military District No. 12, Regina:

This will acknowledge your telephone conversation of a short time ago, advising us that it is the intention of the dominion government to cancel the lease on the above Weyburn property to take effect November 30th, 1941.
The writer had some conversation with you regarding the removal of your improvements and other matters per your lease with this company, feeling that this work could perhaps be done at a later date.
The wrriter took this matter up with Chicago office, and we are to-day in receipt of their letter, which states in part as follows:
We have discussed this matter, and it is our feeling that the terms of the lease should be complied with whenever the government vacates the building.""
War Appropriation
Unless the government intends to continue their occupancy of this building, all of the provisions of the lease should be complied with immediately.
This will confirm our telephone conversation of to-day regarding this matter.
Yours very truly,
A. P. Brown

This indicates that the headquarters of the company refused to carry out the suggestion which had been made in the course of the conversation, that the building might be allowed to remain idle and the improvements not removed. I trust that this will clear the matter up in the mind of my hon. friend. He had the impression, and gave it to the house, that the company had offered to waive the terms of the lease and not require the expenditure to be made.

The hon. member for Peel asked a question with regard to categories of the reserve army. My information is that instructions covering enlistment into the reserve army allow category C men to be accepted. Men, however, between the ages of nineteen and thirty-five who are category A or B cannot be enlisted unless they are (a) those who have been granted or would: be entitled to postponement of compulsory training under the National Resources Mobilization Act; (b) members of Canadian officers' training corps of military age until graduation, also cannot be enlisted in the reserve army.

One other point which was mentioned, and which perhaps is not important, but it struck me rather forcibly and with some surprise, was with regard to the quantity of socks purchased by the department. The hon. member for Peterborough West quoted, I believe, from the report of the Department of Munitions and Supply to the effect that ten million pairs of woollen socks had been purchased. It sounded like a large amount, but the explanation is very simple. The quantity ordered since September, 1939, is 10,168,000 pairs. There have been actually issued to personnel of the active and reserve force units and to troops proceeding overseas since that time 5,336,364 pairs, leaving 4,831,636 pairs which have been ordered but which have not been issued. There were shipped overseas for the Canadian troops in the last year

column2: pairs, leaving 4,205,636 pairs, and of these there are in stock 1,384,988 pairs, and there are due in outstanding orders which have not been delivered, 2,820,648 pairs. That information is given as of March 27, so that although there were 10,168,000 pairs ordered, of these roughly 1,300,000 were in stock and
had not been delivered.

1263901,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.5,1942-04-22,6dec82d6-fab3-438b-b40f-c7720a93d8c1,ca.m.5451,Mr. GREEN:,,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,Within the last few days articles have appeared in the press to the effect that a change is being made in the type of training being given to the men in the army. It would be helpful if the minister would explain. those changes. It does seem of the utmost importance that the army should be so trained that every man may be a fighter. I doubt very much whether that is the position at the present time. I believe there are men in the active army in Canada who have no rifles-if I am wrong I wish the minister would correct me-and certainly men who have had no rifle training. It is of the utmost importance that these men should be so trained. At any rate, the main consideration should be to train them in fighting. The Australian commander in Malaya, Major-General Henry Gordon Bennett, when he escaped after the fall of Singapore and returned to Australia, had this to say, as reported in the Ottawa Journal of March 16:
He charged that what he called barrack-square methods of training took the initiative out of troops.

It does seem that there is still quite a lot of the 1918 complex in connection with the training of our troops. Could the minister give us a statement to-day as to what changes have recently been made in the training of our troops?

,National Government,,Richard Burpee Hanson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9befc64-819d-4523-8a07-915e74257442&Language=E&Section=ALL
1263904,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.8,1942-04-22,1e31f4aa-36bd-40a6-a784-7d94f0e97979,ca.m.7675,Mr. RALSTON:,Minister of National Defence,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,My hon. friend is quite right; it is an important factor. However, the trial has been made and the results have been seen. There is no doubt that men who have seen troops actively at work, actively engaged, who have been trained in training centres, are of one mind with respect to the desirability and the necessity of training in that way. There are, of course, constant changes in details of training. What might be called the frills in connection with drill are cut out; nevertheless most of these things have to be done if a man is to be made an efficient soldier and if discipline and smartness are to be maintained. By smartness I do not mean simply appearance for parade purposes, but alacrity, accuracy, energy, initiative, resourcefulness and readiness to obey an order. When I was over there, No. 1 unit was brushing up, had been in the line for, I think, six or eight weeks and had come out and was taking some individual training again; others were taking section training, they were going on with platoon training. The training depends on the divisional commander and the length of time they have been away from active training.

1263956,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.60,1942-04-22,1e31f4aa-36bd-40a6-a784-7d94f0e97979,ca.m.7675,Mr. RALSTON:,Minister of National Defence,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,WTe are endeavouring to

make the establishment large enough so that fatigues may be avoided or reduced and the time spent practically entirely in connection with training. I must say that there are some objections as well as some advantages in that, because I have always felt that one part of a soldier's training was doing a certain amount of what are called fatigue duties, which are routine duties which would have to be performed if a soldier were on active service, just as they have to be performed in camp. But it has been felt that the training syllabus is so full that it is desirable to spend every possible moment on training. As my hon. friend probably knows, the training time is run off hour after hour, and there is barely enough time for soldiers to get the full training laid down in the syllabus at the basic and advanced training centres, without taking time for fatigue duties.

They say it is just as much part of their training as the marching up and down the streets of which we see so much these days. I think there is something sound in that. They have to do this fatigue duty if
War Appropriation

they are on active service; so why should they not do their fair share of it in the training centres? That is the- theory which has been sold to me. I do not want to give it as mine at all, but I suggest that there is a great deal of sound common sense behind it.

1263958,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.62,1942-04-22,1e31f4aa-36bd-40a6-a784-7d94f0e97979,ca.m.7675,Mr. RALSTON:,Minister of National Defence,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,As I intimated, I had

It only means that the time at the training centre is fully occupied with the syllabus that has been laid down.

1263963,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.67,1942-04-22,d34eb71d-3bc8-4258-8a3f-2007fa662c38,ca.m.4292,Mr. DOUGLAS (Weyburn):,,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,First I want to thank the minister for the information he gave the committee and myself, since I was particularly interested, with regard to the Weyburn barracks. I am glad to learn that the fault did not lie primarily with the government, but that the offer made by the manager was not endorsed by the headquarters of his company in Chicago. But I want to point out to the committee that this does not entirely dispose of the case; it means simply that the responsibility has been shifted. Here is a very excellent building, one of the best for use as a barracks anywhere in Saskatchewan, or probably anywhere in western Canada. It is standing idle at a time when we are putting up new buildings in other parts of the country. Under a lease we were paying, I believe, $560 a month in rent, and I agree that there would be no sense in the world in paying that amount of money if we were not using the building. Apparently the company were not prepared to abide by the offer made by their manager, that as long as the building was not being used no rent should be paid, but that the equipment put into the building by
the government should remain there pending the time when it might be necessary to use that barracks again, when the rent would commence once more.

As the minister has .pointed out, the company were not prepared to abide by that suggestion; but I should like to know why we have a National Resources Mobilization Act. In June, 1940, legislation was introduced in this house with a great fanfare. The government were going to start to do things; they were going to start taking over things, if they needed them. Here is an excellent three-story building, owned by a United States firm which has not used it for a great many years and is not likely to use it for a good many years more. It seems to me that the government would have been well within its rights in saying to that firm, ""At some future date we may require this building. As a matter of fact, if we ever have to mobilize the second battalion of the South Saskatchewan regiment we shall require it, because it is the only place between Regina and the international boundary where in any emergency we can quickly assemble and equip five hundred or a thousand men. As long as that building is there, and since you do not require it, we propose to leave in it the equipment already there, and1 we will pay you rent only when we use the building."" Under the National Resources Mobilization Act the government has power to do this. To me it seems a pity that we should spend $1,800 or $2,000 in taking out plumbing fixtures and equipment, since undoubtedly the day will come when we shall have to use that building again, when all that equipment will have to be put back. Therefore, while I am glad to have the statement by the minister that the firm did not support the suggestion made by their manager, certainly I think the government would have been well advised and quite within its rights in insisting that the offer should have been endorsed by the company.

I wanted to ask the minister one or two questions, the first arising out of what has been said' by the hon. member for Vancouver South with reference to the men on active service carrying on duties which do not ordinarily require them to carry rifles. I refer to orderlies, truck drivers, chauffeurs, clerks and so on. What is the minimum training that is given to all men in active service, in rifle and machine gun work? In other words, I take it for granted that the same procedure is followed as in the air force, where, no matter to wihat branch a man is sent, he is given a certain minimum training in the use of small
War Appropriation

arms. I think it would1 clarify the situation if the minister would tell us what is the minimum training that a man on active service must have in small arms, irrespective of what he is doing. The minister also speaks of there [DOT]being rifles for all these men, and I take it for granted that this means Lee-Enfieldi rifles. One of the minister's secretaries was kind enough to send me some information with reference to the other rifles being used, mainly American, such as Edison, Winchester and various other makes which we generally class as Springfield. They are manufactured by different firms, but they come under the Springfield classification in that they are of [DOT]300 calibre. I imagine those will be used principally by reserve units, by these guerilla bands which are being set up in the west or by the veterans' guard. I wonder whether, when the minister says there are rifles for all these men, he means Lee-Enfield rifles of -303 calibre.

Would the minister explain to the committee what disposition is made of these men when they come out of the training centres? There have been some two hundred thousand or more men go through these training camps. Are they attached to active service units for further training? Are they brigaded into the division, or just what disposition is made of them after they finish at the training centres?
I
column2: should be glad also if the minister would be kind enough to outline the new plans that have been hinted at with reference to the reserve army. I understand that some of the reserve units are now being brigaded; that there is to be an increase in the period of training and an intensification of the training of these reserve units. Would the minister outline the plans of his department in regard to the reserve army?

1263974,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.78,1942-04-22,1e31f4aa-36bd-40a6-a784-7d94f0e97979,ca.m.7675,Mr. RALSTON:,Minister of National Defence,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,The reserve army is part of the defence scheme of Canada; it forms a second line in that respect. They consist not only of infantry, but also of artillery, medical corps, ordnance corps and all the auxiliary services which should go to make up a brigade group.

I had the interesting experience of attending meetings with the officers commanding the reserve brigade groups in three districts- No. 11 at Vancouver, No. 6 at Halifax and No. 7 at Saint John. We have explained to them as fully as possible what we can do, having regard to the allocation of equipment which is necessary in the times in which we live and in the emergency which exists. Equipment from Canadian factories does not by any means all go to Canadian troops; it goes to practically every field and every active front that there is. We have explained to them the situation. These reserve brigade groups will train as reserve units at their own armouries or local headquarters. They will go to camp for fifteen days during the summer. I think it was the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) who asked about the training of the reserve army. We expect not to dwell so much on individual training but to endeavour to see that the men who come there are dealt with along lines of training which will interest them and which will in as little time as possible give them the rudiments of
fMr. Ualston.]
soldiering and some of the basic principles which are needed in connection with organization and serving in units.

1263978,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.82,1942-04-22,d34eb71d-3bc8-4258-8a3f-2007fa662c38,ca.m.4292,Mr. DOUGLAS (Weyburn):,,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,I do not want to labour this question of the barracks; but it certainly comes veiy poorly from the minister, after saying that my argument is fallacious, to proceed to make the most specious argument imaginable, that a legal contract stands in the way of their use to-day when this country is at war. ,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Thomas Clement (Tommy) Douglas,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d34eb71d-3bc8-4258-8a3f-2007fa662c38&Language=E&Section=ALL
1263981,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.85,1942-04-22,795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1,ca.m.1278,Mr. GRAYDON:,,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,There are one or two matters upon which I feel compelled to speak this afternoon, and I do so with reluctance for two reasons. One is that I can scarcely pose as an expert in the matters now under discussion, and the second is that any man with a keen sense of responsibility towards our war effort must be extremely careful in any statements he makes about the armed forces. With those considerations in mind I bring two points to the minister's attention.

On March 18 the Prime Minister made his statement with regard to the establishment of unity of command in three areas of defence in Canada-one on the Pacific coast, one on the Atlantic coast and one in Newfoundland. The choice of commander for each of these unified areas in the final analysis rested with the senior officer in that area in charge of one or other branch of our armed forces. I can make no comment which would be of any use to the committee with respect to the eligibility or usefulness of any of these three men, but I would bring to the attention of the committee reflections which one hears of public opinion from time to time, and that is, the public are anxious to know whether the appointments to positions of supreme importance in our national defence and in our national waging of this war are to be made strictly from the point of view of seniority of service or whether other factors which the public, rightly or wrongly, believes to be of importance are to be taken into account.

I point out to the minister the danger, of which he is already aware, of paying much attention to armchair critics of our war effort. I should not like to think that the minister would pay much attention to them. But one is compelled as a member of parliament at least to bring to the attention of the government what one hears among the public from

time to time, so that if there is a germ of constructive suggestion in their ideas they may be adopted, not only with a view to increasing the efficiency of our armed forces but to improve the morale of the people for whom these forces are fighting.

While I hesitate to suggest that the element of seniority should be entirely disregarded with regard to appointments, may I urge upon the minister that in appointments particularly to positions of major importance, some measure of significance be attached to knowledge of the newest and latest types of warfare. I believe that the minister, the forces and the people of Canada all realize that it is not enough even to have men well trained with respect to methods of war as practised in 1939. Since that time, methods of waging war and the character of the war itself have changed so much that it taxes the best brains of the war offices in every one of the united nations to keep up to date as regards the instruments and style of warfare to be used.

What I am saying, as the minister will understand, is a reflection of opinions which have been expressed not only to myself, but, I am sure, to most hon. members. Most of us, including myself, are anxious that nothing we say shall be a reflection upon those who are commanding our armed forces in this country or elsewhere. But in Great Britain they have not hesitated to criticize, in the interests of the nation. Men of major standing in public life have done so; they have called for an end of what they term the Colonel Blimp mentality in their national war effort. I have not come to this chamber for the purpose of charging that we in Canada have any such mentality, but I want the minister to understand that in the interests of the forces and of the public a careful scrutiny should be made and a thorough survey instituted, by himself, or by someone else competent to do so, so that the public shall be satisfied that our forces are controlled and led by men who are up to date with regard to modern warfare; in other words, that the Canadian forces are led by the best brains and the most efficient men whom Canada can produce, regardless of whether they are of senior or junior standing. I am supported in this argument by what has been said by General McNaughton himself. If anything in the past few months has encouraged and strengthened the morale of the general public, it is that General McNaughton in his press relations has made mention of this very fact which I am trying, though inadequately, to put before this committee. He has said that younger men, men who have
IVar Appropriation
had experience in modern warfare, will be given responsible positions regardless of age or other circumstances which, though in peace time they may mean a great deal, in war time mean very little.

I have brought these matters to the minister's attention reluctantly and1 with much hesitation. I believe, however, he is entitled to know that there is a section of public opinion which would like some assurance from him that everything possible has been done to see to it that the men appointed to take command of our Canadian units have the aggressive mentality necessary to wage the sort of total warfare which is being employed against us by our enemies.

A word with regard to the training itself. I do not want the minister to answer this question if it would disclose something which should not be revealed, but it seems to me that the manual and the course used- for the training of our armed forces, particularly our officers, though it may have been useful twenty years ago or even three or four years ago, may not be of as much effect to-day having regard to the kaleidoscopic changes which have taken place. I suggest that every possible effort be made to modernize our training to the very last minute. I want to see the Canadian army second to none in the world so far as up-to-date, efficient, offensive methods are concerned. The Canadian people have a right to expect that; as a member of parliament I hope that is what they have, and I am not suggesting otherwise. But I would emphasize as strongly as I can that the minister set aside everything in our training which may be obsolete, and apply to the training of our armed forces the methods of to-day.
I believe he will understand the spirit which moves me to make these suggestions, and on behalf of the Canadian people I urge that he give all possible consideration to them.

1263982,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.86,1942-04-22,1e31f4aa-36bd-40a6-a784-7d94f0e97979,ca.m.7675,Mr. RALSTON:,Minister of National Defence,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,My hon. friend speaks,

if I may say so to him, as a man after my own heart. There is not anything that he has said with which I find the slightest fault. I have said in this house and I say to this committee that I do not regard seniority as being a governing factor in connection with appointments to commands.

He has mentioned the three combined commands, those of the Atlantic, the Pacific, and Newfoundland. It happened there that the senior officers were regarded as well qualified. They were appointed on that ground and, having taken counsel not only with those who are immediately around me, but with others as well, I shall be tremendously disappointed if that confidence is not justified. I

am not going to deal with individuals, because that would be invidious. But Major-General Page, in Newfoundland, went to England and was there for some time; he went to Iceland, and afterwards, as hon. members know, took command of the fourth division. Major-General Alexander is a soldier of very long experience and a splendid record, which I will not relate here. I had an opportunity of seeing him at the Pacific coast, discussing matters with him and being around with him a great deal in connection with Pacific coast matters, and from what I learned and saw of how the three services are cooperating, while one will never be fully satisfied, I had every reason to believe that the appointment made and the decision come to by the war committee of the cabinet was eminently satisfactory. On the Atlantic coast, Major-General Elkins happened to be the senior man there. He had a splendid record in the last war. He filled several important posts in Canada and we were very glad to be able to avail ourselves of his services when the Atlantic command was established on the east coast, and found evidence of excellent cooperation between him and his colleagues of the other two services. It must be remembered that both these officers have officers in their command who have been overseas in this war, and know the conditions and the needs there both in training and operation.

Further than that, in connection with training-and this is what I want to emphasize- with all these units in Canada beginning with the second division, because the first division had to be trained by men who had not been overseas in this war, we have followed the policy of asking for men to be returned from England as brigadiers to command divisions. General McNaughton went with the first division and Major-General Odium with the second division, and some of his brigadiers, two out of three, I think, were men who had been overseas. Major-General Price commanded the third division. He was brought back from overseas. He was not selected on the ground of seniority. He was not the senior by any means, but was given command of the third division on the recommendation of his senior officer who knew him and who believed that he would fit the job. Major-General Page was recommended for the fourth division in exactly the same way. He was not senior, but a brigadier in charge of holding units at that time. He had been in Iceland and in England and had been in charge of holding units there, and he was sent here on the recommendation of General McNaughton. Major-General Sansom who commands the fifth division was not senior but was brought
War Appropriation

back on the recommendation of his senior officer, who believed that he was best fitted for the job. Lieutenant-General Crerar had been in England three times in this war. He was first the senior officer at Canadian military headquarters in England and had done a splendid job for about a year in connection with the setting up of Canadian headquarters and, as well, in connection with the organization of the whole Canadian effort there. Lieutenant-General Crerar is a professional soldier, a staff officer of wide attainments and a man who has not simply administrative ability. He has a fine training on the general staff side as well. He was selected to command the second division and he is now commanding the Canadian corps. In every case without exception recommendations have come from overseas for the men who have been placed at the head of our formations, and that course is being followed in connection with the sixth, seventh and eighth divisions. The commanders of these will be announced in due course.

In connection with brigadiers, I have not at the moment a list before me, and I have not been able to recall them all, but I think at least two out of three in every case were men who had had service overseas and had come back with training and operational experience gained there. In addition to that, the brigadier in charge of training to-day is Brigadier Weeks, who was overseas for two years, and with him is Lieutenant-Colonel Sparling, who was overseas for a year and was brought back. The quartermaster-general is Major-General MacKenzie who was brought here from overseas.

The armoured corps, which is being trained at the present time, is being trained under the direction of officers from the other side. We had to get British officers in the first place in order that the suggestion made by my hon. friend would be carried out, namely, that the men would get the benefit of the latest experience in connection with operations and the latest methods of training. There are now over 1,000 personnel brought back within the last two months to carry on training in connection with the extended army programme.

1263984,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.88,1942-04-22,1e31f4aa-36bd-40a6-a784-7d94f0e97979,ca.m.7675,Mr. RALSTON:,Minister of National Defence,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,Officers and non-commissioned officers. My hon. friend refers to the training of officers. We have put in charge of the training of officers at Brockville the Sergeant-at-Arms of this house, Colonel Gregg, V.C., who has returned after a splendid career overseas. He is now coming to take charge of the officers' training centre at Brockville. Colonel Scott of the Calgary Highlanders has come back to take charge of the senior officers' course. This indicates that we are trying to

meet the specification which my hon. friend lays down, namely, to secure people who know what the latest types of training and operations are, and it means also that we are meeting the specifications which must be satisfactory to General McNaughton, or he would not agree to the junior war staff course coming back here. The officers' training course has been eminently satisfactory. These men who have come here have proved satisfactory, and the cadets will get the benefit of the experience and training of Colonel Gregg, V.C., who comes from the O.C.T.U., as they call it over there, of which he has been in charge in England.

resolution go through without bringing to the attention of the Minister of National Defence and the members of this committee, particularly those from the Pacific coast, the fact that there is another section of Canada vitally interested in our war activities. I have in mind the Atlantic coast, more particularly the coast of Nova Scotia. Paragraph (d) of the resolution reads:
The carrying out of any measures deemed necessary or advisable by the governor in council in consequence of the existence of a state of war.

Some time ago the city of Halifax, which is part of the province of Nova Scotia, made representations to the Canadian National Railways for the improvement of the underpass on the main road to Debert and other sections to the north and northwest. They did this largely because of the need for bringing in reinforcements should there be an attack on the Atlantic coast centering around Halifax. I remember quite well the explosion which occurred in the harbour of Halifax in 1917 when something like 1,700 lives were lost. It was caused by a collision of two boats at a point where only one should have been. You all recall what that meant to the port of Halifax and the people of Halifax. A similar occurrence could very well take place at the present time. We all hope it will not happen, but it is quite possible. I remember at that time the roads were blocked and it was impossible to bring into the city the doctors, nurses and others who were anxious to give assistance to those who were injured.

An officer commanding a unit in mlitary district No. 6 has stated that reinforcements could not be brought in sufficiently quickly to help to defend the port of Halifax, largely because the railway and the road could become blocked or be put out of business by sabotage. It is in this connection that I direct the attention of the Minister of National Defence to the necessity of placing

at the disposal of either the Canadian National Railways or the Department of Munitions and Supply sufficient funds to remedy this dangerous hazard which now exists, the underpass entrance at Fairview.

The city of Halifax felt that the Canadian National Railway was the proper body to deal with this matter, but a great many persons in Halifax and Nova Scotia, including myself, feel that it is really a matter of defence. I think all members of this committee realize that Halifax is playing a large part in the transporting of goods, munitions and troops overseas. If anything were to happen to prevent the reshipment of goods abroad brought in by rail to the city of Halifax, it would be a calamity so far as the empire is concerned.

This underpass is on the main artery leading into the city. As I stated a moment ago, if we were so unfortunate as to have , an attack I doubt very much whether troops could be brought in from Debert and other points quickly enough to give assistance to the defenders of Halifax. The estimate of the cost of doing this work is $137,500. Application was made to the Canadian National Railways, but the learned counsel who represented the railway company presented such a good argument that the commission decided it was not within their jurisdiction that they should spend this amount. They claimed that it was the duty of the provincial highway authorities to provide an artery sufficiently wide to carry troops to the city of Halifax. I urge the minister to take this matter into his serious consideration with a view to placing at the disposal of the proper authorities a sufficient sum to provide an artery wide enough for the transport of troops should the occasion arise when that will be necessary.

I should also like to express the thought which I believe is in the minds of a great many, if not all of those associated with the defence of the Atlantic area, concerning the commanding officers. On two occasions in this house the question was raised as to whether these men were qualified. I feel that I am expressing the thought of all in that area when I say that we are perfectly satisfied with those who have been placed in charge of the defence of the Atlantic coast. We are familiar with the background of those men, not only the officer commanding but those associated with him in the army, the navy, and the air force. We on the Atlantic coast are satisfied that these men are making a pretty good job of the work which has been assigned to them.
I should like to ask a question with regard to the reserve army officers. I do not know

whether the officers of the reserve units are men who have volunteered for active service overseas or purely for home defence. The reserve army itself is set up for home defence, but I should like to know whether the officers of the reserve units at some time or another have volunteered for active service overseas.

In closing, may I urge the minister not to evade the question I have raised with respect to a sufficiently wide artery into Halifax- of course, I know the minister is not in the habit of evading questions or evading responsibility. What I mean is that I do not want him simply to say that the improvement of the main artery or road or underpass, or whatever he chooses to term it, is a question for some other body than the Department of National Defence. I feel that this work is so essential to the proper carrying on of our war activities that the minister should give it his very serious consideration.

1264030,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.134,1942-04-22,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,I should like to bring two or three matters to the minister's attention. He has been very obliging in supplying a lot of information that I wanted to get.

First, I would ask him in reference to the agreement which I understand is going to be signed in Toronto to-morrow about the use of the Canadian National exhibition grounds. The city of Toronto has spent about twenty-four million dollars on the grounds and buildings and permanent exhibits, and in view of that I think the minister should be good enough to make a survey and see whether the troops from the chief recruiting district in Canada, Toronto, cannot be housed in those grounds, as well as recruits from the neighbouring cities and towns. Toronto soldiers have been sent all over the country from Halifax to Vancouver. I wish to be helpful to the minister because I appreciate the great difficulties that anyone must have in operating a war department at this time. But I would say this, that in the last war recruiting was very greatly helped by having the home units stationed near their homes, where their families could see them, and their friends, many of whom they persuaded to join the colours. That policy wras one of the greatest incentives to recruiting that we had in the last war. The minister was in the great war, and I appreciate what he did then in the matter of recruiting. The Toronto exhibition grounds comprise nearly four hundred acres. There
IFar Appropriation

is also the waterfront and the Ontario government's magnificent Elizabeth highway; the land on both sides of that 'highway is practically vacant. All this area could be used for military purposes, for the accommodation of all the regiments in southern Ontario. It is unnecessary to spend a large amount of money on another camp if proper use is made of those grounds. I hope the minister will consider the agreement with the city of Toronto and accommodate the troops of Toronto and southern Ontario in the Toronto area.

My second point is with reference to transportation. The minister a year ago brought down a return which showed that up to the end of 1940 the Canadian Pacific railway had received $2,750,000 and the Canadian National railway $2,500,000 out of the war, or pretty nearly as much as they made out of the whole four and a half years of the last war. What kind of treatment have the soldiers obtained from the railways? I travel on the trains. I have taken this matter up with the minister, and he did make some effort to get the railways to improve their soldier rolling stock.

While travelling on the railways, I see hockey, baseball, and other United States teams from across the border and touring amusement and theatrical companies pulling up in front of the stations in luxurious cars on Canada's American end of our railways on a railway paid for by the people of this country, and yet we cannot get proper rolling stock in Ontario to carry the troops. On one train I saw a car at the back with Royal Air Force boys, some having come from as far as London and from all over the Toronto district. What do they think when they see two or three luxurious coaches devoted to the use of some of the people who stay at home to whom I referred, while they themselves are packed in like a lot of sardines on an old used coach? Talk about Toronto's street railway and the overcrowding under private ownership! I have seen nothing to equal this. When troops who have to come from as far as Vancouver and Halifax receive such treatment, before another dollar is voted for betterments in this house to the railways I intend to ask for and have a showdown. The railways are making fabulous sums out of the war by the transportation of troops, munitions and food, and the people of Canada are not getting value for troop transportation. I admit that the minister sent me a reply he got last summer from the railways, promising improvements, but that was almost a year ago, and nothing much better has yet been done.

I urge the government to insist on some improvement along the line I have indicated. Soldiers should have free passage on the railroads. It is unjust and unfair to send Toronto men, who should be accommodated at the exhibition grounds in Toronto, as far away as Vancouver or the eastern seaboard, or a few over to Labrador, where they cannot get home for six months and where the cost of transportation may be as high as $180. At the same time we have a pass system under which, according to the last Duff report, 687,000 passes were granted on the two railways. Unfortunately I am not able to be a soldier, but I plead for them, and I say that a showdown is called for. I admit that the board of transport commissioners has no jurisdiction over railway companies for soldier fares in war time; under the Railway Act they have not that power; but they or some other body should be given the power or authorized to enforce what I have suggested. Trains are being run now to Camp Borden- a camp on which, I venture to say, if the present minister had been minister at the time, $7,000,000 would never have been spent. I have called it an ice-box in the winter and a hot-box in the summer, and that is exactly what it is. There was no necessity of moving so many local troops out there when we have in Toronto the exhibition grounds, when we have the Elizabeth highway, and in view of the munificent help which the Ontario government has given to the extension of their highway system. It costs $1.95 to $2.05 to go to Camp Borden on a week-end; and if there are say, three children, half-fare must be paid, or more than a week's pay to the soldier is taken from the wife and family for one visit to Camp Borden. At the same time hitch-hiking on the road has been stopped. No wonder recruiting is handicapped. I notice the Minister of Finance in his seat. I sympathize with him in a great many ways; he has shown much patience towards some hon. members; but I must say I am very sorry that he could not see his way to aid recruiting and help the Minister of National Defence in carrying on the burden of the war by giving soldiers' dependents a cost-of-living bonus, the same as civilians get who draw around $175 a month.

Another matter to which I wish to refer is the women's army. I hold in my hand a copy of a debate of forty-six pages in the British House of Commons, sent to me by a British member of parliament who is interested in women's efforts as applied to the war. There was a long debate in the British house on March 6 of this year. I have written for three or four more copies of this report to
War Appropriation

give to the leaders in the house. I hope that the minister and his deputy will study this question, and have time to read of what the women of Britain are doing to win the war. In my opinion a committee of the house should be appointed to study this whole question; it might include our two lady members and others of women's services. What are the women of Britain doing? In the course of the debate a British woman minister refers to the fact that in Birmingham, or Manchester, some women with three or four children are screening coal. Every woman in England is conscripted and is engaged in some war work. I do not urge that that should be the case in this country, but I believe that if the minister will study this question-and he has given it a lot of thought-he will learn how women's efforts could be greatly increased. Take the pay service, where male civilians as soldiers are employed; their work, or much of it, could be done by women, because it is done by women very well and efficiently in private industry. Note also how British women are transported to the munitions plants, and how dozens of government hostels have been erected all over the country in every district to take care of the children, the cost being borne by the government. While their children are being cared for, the women of England are engaged in the munitions plants and in all forms of production and in all kinds of work, whereas here it often happens that street cars are not available, nor are our women escorted to work and back, as they are in the old country. After all, women constitute 50 per cent of the population and will have to bear their share of paying for the war and the suffering of their children. Yet what they have had to put up with in the homes bombed and destroyed, with their soldier husbands away, is intolerable; they must look after their children, send them to school, provide them with meals, and many of them cannot keep body and soul together because of the high cost of living and lack of a bonus.

I wish to refer to one other matter. I do not think the minister will take objection to my remarks about the troops who got into trouble at Halifax. It is due to no fault of the minister, and I have already referred to the lack of equipment on the railways and his active efforts to better things. After two and a half years of war, surely a railway corporation, so well equipped with some luxury trains to which I have referred, or steamship company, can afford better accommodation for our troops. After all the people of this country have done for the railways and for shipping, they should be expected to treat our

troops decently in land and ocean services. I have in mind the complaints of those who came from Vancouver to Halifax. I believe that the large majority of those young fellows wanted to obey the law, and I regret that we are not better provided with ships and railway cars. I know something about the navigation business. I was chairman of and a member of a harbour board in those capacities for twenty-seven years; I have taken a great interest in the waterfront and in shipping. Unfortunately the Canadian National Railways and the merchant marine sold some of our finest vessels for $10,000 each. I know of ships which were built for war service in the last war, costing one and a half to one and three quarter millions apiece, which were sold for a mere nothing. The history of shipping in the five years before the war discloses a deplorable state of affairs. Largely owing to the rate of taxation in England, it was not unusual a few months before the war to see in the British newspapers pages of advertisements offering boats for as low as $50,000. Liners sold for taxes. A number of the ships, the Prince line, which the Canadian National Railways disposed of for about $10,000 could now have been used to transport our troops. I had a return of these ships of the merchant marine and the cost and sale price thereof.

In the last war there was an inquiry with reference to the Dardanelles expedition and the Mesopotamia affair which revealed a shocking state regarding the troops. The minister himself is a soldier with a very fine record, and I know he is a man of keen personal sympathies. Although I am not here to speak on and know nothing of the Halifax incident, I think there should be some further inquiry and some action taken in this matter, and I hope due consideration will be given to fair and most lenient treatment of these men, because nobody sitting up here in an office should give orders regarding an incident of this kind at Halifax until there has been a proper investigation into the cause and effect, and proper transports afforded. I hope the inquiry will relate to the conditions under which these troops are labouring in transit, and also why, after two and a half years of war, we have not adequate transportation for war purposes on land and sea.

On Saturday night I stood at the corner of Queen and Yonge streets in Toronto. I saw a great many soldiers in the air force and the army, and along came five or six ladies, officers of the women's army, and these men had to salute them. The whole principle of saluting, except on parade, should be abolished. I fail to see the common sense of soldiers who are going overseas being
War Appropriation

obliged to salute those not going overseas, or women troops. I was with a young soldier last Saturday night, a fellow who had been thirty-six times over Germany and who has now been transferred to the west coast. These are the men who have gone overseas and have been doing the fighting. Why should young soldiers in the air force and the other forces, like this young gentleman, have to salute a lot of people who are only civilian soldiers or, as a British member once called them ""glorified civilians""? I am not here to criticize any man wearing the king's uniform; they deserve our praise, but I do suggest that the saluting business in principle is carried too far and except on parade it might well be abolished or curtailed. At any rate, some new, modern regulation should be made to govern this matter. I fail to see why veterans of the great war and this, and non-commissioned officers should be required to salute a lady. Every man salutes a lady in the proper way by taking off his hat, but I repeat, this saluting should be abolished or properly controlled.

I salute the minister and say to him that I hope he will go after this transportation question with which I have dealt and do something with the railways in order to improve conditions. Dear knows, improvements I suggested are badly needed. When I came here first we had a debate for six months on the question of the shipping combine in the Atlantic off Halifax. I do not know what sort of regulation we have in this war time. There was a long debate when I first came here on that shipping combine in the Atlantic and on improving it, and I do hope that this whole question will be further investigated.

No one can say more for the Toronto units than I do. They are equal or almost equal to the 85th Battalion in the last war, and I should like to see some of these fine Toronto units in Toronto. What we are planning on is having the grounds used as a proper depot, because I must say for the Toronto district,

and district No. 2 generally, that I think they have carried on under as difficult conditions, so far as accommodation is concerned, as any district in Canada and have done a splendid job in connection with recruiting, notwithstanding that. We want to provide a better type of accommodation, and the exhibition grounds will give us an opportunity to do so. With regard to transportation, the hon. member ihas been the champion of the soldiers, so far as transportation fares are concerned, from the beginning of the war. I do not think I am justified in holding out any hope with regard to revision of that matter.

Every scrap of rolling stock that can be used is being utilized, being shuttled back and forth from central Canada to the Atlantic coast, and as my hon. friend knows, the car shops are busy in the making not only of cars but of munitions of war. Conditions are not ideal in connection with transportation, but I do think that so far as the army is concerned there has been a slight improvement owing to the fact that a change has been -made in the matter of accommodation so that there is now no discrimination as between the army and the air force.

The hon. member speaks of hockey teams and I agree with him. He also refers to theatre companies. But if you had as many hockey teams and theatre companies travelling as soldiers you would have to provide tourist accommodation for them as well as for the soldiers. It is a question of lack of rolling stock.

1264042,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.146,1942-04-22,62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443,ca.m.5390,Mr. GILLIS:,,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,Most of the discussion this afternoon has centred on one end of the country. I had no desire to take part in the discussion, but it would appear to anyone reading the record that in regard to the question of defence we are concerned about only one end of the country. I was pleased to see one hon. member rise in his place and make some observations regarding Halifax. But I do not think he touched on the important thing so far as Halifax is concerned. I spent a week or so there within the last month, and I think the greatest danger Halifax is confronted with is the congestion that exists in the city. There has been perhaps a doubling of the population and nothing has been done with respect to establishing services to care for the increase. It is impossible to get a meal; it is impossible to get a room in a hotel. In that city there are large numbers of troops from all over the country, and naturally their families want to be with them. The rents that these airmen, sailors and soldiers are obliged to pay is something terrible, and that is one question which I think the minister should take under consideration.
War Appropriation

I believe a large part of the population of Halifax is non-essential, and should not be there. If there is no accommodation for the families of men who are obliged to live there, they should be made acquainted with that situation, so that their families would not be taken from one end of the country to the other to create the congestion that exists in that city to-day. In my opinion Halifax is in the worst shape of any city I have ever been in; anything could happen there. The question raised by another hon. member, as to getting people out of the city, is important and should be attended to; but I believe the influx of people into Halifax at the present time is a matter that should be taken under advisement as well. I heard some terrible stories in Halifax, stories which I would not want to repeat publicly. Perhaps the minister knows all about them, but according to the information I obtained there, from sources I consider reliable, things certainly are not in good shape.

Of course Halifax is not Nova Scotia, though a great many people think it is. In the other end of the province there is a large section where they are making fairly good strides with regard to organization for air raid precautions work and all that sort of thing. But there is one matter which I do not think has been considered. Most of the collieries of Cape Breton island are located right on the coast. I do not know whether representations have been made to the department in this connection, but for sixteen hours a day you have working in many of these collieries approximately a thousand men. They are a thousand feet under ground, some of them five miles out under the Atlantic ocean. With one shell a ship near that coast could knock down the bankhead and entomb a thousand men, and it would not have to be a very large shell, either. The miners realize this, and no doubt this would be one of the first things an enemy ship would try to do. I know the men have been taking up this matter with the companies for some considerable time, but to the best of my knowledge very little progress has been made. This I think is another matter the department should take under advisement.

Then there is the question of promotions in the arm}', the establishment of officers. On several occasions in the house the minister has stated that this time the army was being formed on a democratic basis; that service and experience were the only things that would count; that men with the necessary qualifications, who went through the basic [Mr. Gillis.l

training, would be promoted and developed into our leaders in this war. I was very glad to hear the minister make those statements, and I should like to believe them to be true. But from the information I obtain, that is not so. If the minister would ride on a regular train from Montreal to Halifax and back again, and talk to the troops on the train, I think he would get a different picture. The story I get is this, that if you enlist, take your basic training and become a non-commissioned officer, you are there for the duration. It is considered bad manners for the rank and file soldier to make application for a commission. I do not know whether or not this is true, but the minister should know. I am told that most of their officers are being pitchforked in from the top. Most of them appear to be college students.

1264046,ca.proc.d.1942-04-22.12.1.150,1942-04-22,62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443,ca.m.5390,Mr. GILLIS:,,WAR APPROPRIATION BILL,PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY,,Refuse to accept men in
industry who have been discharged from the army as medically unfit. I have met numbers of boys who have told me, ""I have
Canada Evidence Act

applied for a job. I have done the best I could. I was in the army for four months""- or eight months, or a year-""and I cannot get a job. I present my discharge certificate, and they tell me it is not worth the paper it is written on. They say they do not want men who are physically unfit, that if I am not fit for the army I am not fit for the work they have to offer."" There are many men running around with discharge certificates, many of whom have had considerable service, unable to get work. The other boys, who would like to enlist, see what happens to these men and say, ""If I get a certificate showing that I am medically unfit I am out of luck as far as work is concerned,"" and they do not enlist. The minister should check up on that matter.

With respect to the question of women in industry, we all agree on this principle, but I think we must be careful to see that the employer does not take advantage of the present situation to weed out many of the men and bring in women at much lower wages. This has been done. Right here in Ontario men who were receiving 80 cents an hour have been shoved out of industries and replaced by women at 35 cents an hour. The principle of employing women in industry is sound, but it should not be followed until there is a shortage of labour, and certainly employers should not be permitted to take advantage of it, as some are doing at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, it is almost six o'clock and I do not want to take up any more time. I did want to make these few observations with respect to the east coast. Matters are in bad shape there, perhaps more so than on the Pacific coast. People are beginning to realize the situation, I believe one great mistake we are making is in our refusal to take the people of the country absolutely into our confidence with respect to the seriousness of the situation. It may be said that to do so would cause fear, or this, that or the other thing. It will not. I think our greatest mistake is in trying to minimize some danger that may be a great deal more serious than the people imagine. You are lulling them to sleep, and if anything should happen they will not be ready for it. If the people are told the absolute truth, with all the cards laid face up on the table, they will go to work with good heart. I know on the island of Cape Breton they are war-minded to-day. The workers themselves are taking the initiative in pushing the employers in connection with many questions. The steel workers, the miners and others are setting up production committees themselves, and so on. They are beginning to realize that the situation is serious, and they are ready to meet it with everything they have. That should be the general policy right across the country.
